content: 1. Expanded searches were conducted across SCI-EXPANDED, SSCI, and A&HCI indexes for all years, focusing on topics related to dried blood spot (DBS) testing, including dried plasma spot testing and related terms. 2. A systematic review and meta-analysis were performed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of hepatitis C virus (HCV) antibody detection using DBS samples compared to venous blood samples. This included searches in MEDLINE, EMBASE, Global Health, and the Cochrane Library. 3. The review followed PRISMA guidelines and used the QUADAS-2 tool to assess the quality and risk of bias in included studies. Observational and interventional studies comparing DBS HCV antibody testing to serum-based testing were included. 4. The pooled analysis revealed a high diagnostic accuracy for DBS testing, with an overall sensitivity of 98% (95% CI: 94–99) and specificity of 99% (95% CI: 97–100). Moderate heterogeneity was observed across studies. 5. Storage conditions did not significantly affect sensitivity or specificity when samples were stored for less than 24 hours at room temperature. However, false positives were reported in two studies when DBS samples were stored at room temperature for more than three days. 6. The review highlighted the lack of standardized cut-offs for DBS testing, as various studies used different assays and thresholds, often determined through receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. 7. The quality of included studies was moderate, with some studies failing to adequately report on key issues such as sampling methods and blinding of laboratory personnel. Only two studies blinded personnel to the reference or index test. 8. The review emphasized the need for manufacturers to validate their tests for DBS use, seek regulatory approval, and include instructions for DBS testing in their manuals. 9. Future research should focus on evaluating the applicability of DBS testing under field conditions, including transport and storage, and on reporting specific cut-offs used with different assays. 10. While DBS testing for HCV antibodies shows good diagnostic accuracy, uncertainties regarding storage conditions and cut-offs limit its broader application in low-resource settings.
